# RID PROTOCOL: Willingness to Pay for School Quality via Boundary Discontinuity Design

## STEP 1 — PRE-COMMITMENT

### Causal Identification Strategy
**Boundary discontinuity design (BDD):** I exploit the spatial discontinuity in school assignment at attendance zone boundaries. The identifying assumption is that houses immediately on either side of an attendance zone boundary share identical neighborhood characteristics (amenities, safety, labor market access, peer effects beyond school) and differ *only* in their assigned school. By comparing log house prices for transactions near the boundary — conditioning on distance to the boundary, housing structural characteristics, and boundary fixed effects — the coefficient on school quality (test scores) identifies the causal willingness-to-pay for school quality.

The running variable is **distance to the nearest attendance zone boundary** (signed: positive = higher-performing school side, negative = lower-performing school side, or used as a continuous control).

### Directional Hypothesis
**Higher school quality (measured by average test scores) causes higher house prices.** Specifically, I hypothesize a positive and statistically significant coefficient on school test scores when estimated via the boundary discontinuity design. I expect the BDD estimate to be **smaller** than the naïve cross-sectional hedonic estimate, because traditional hedonic regressions confound school quality with omitted neighborhood quality (upward bias).

---

## STEP 2 — SPECIFICATION DISCIPLINE

I pre-commit to exactly **5 specifications**, no more:

| Spec | Model | Purpose |
|------|-------|---------|
| **S1** | Naïve hedonic: log(price) ~ test_scores + housing_chars + census_controls | Benchmark OLS without boundary design |
| **S2** | BDD baseline: log(price) ~ test_scores + housing_chars + boundary_FE | Core BDD with boundary fixed effects, full sample |
| **S3** | BDD with bandwidth restriction: Same as S2 but restricted to houses within 0.20 miles of boundary | Tighter bandwidth to strengthen identification |
| **S4** | BDD with linear distance control: log(price) ~ test_scores + housing_chars + boundary_FE + f(distance) | Controls for smooth function of distance to boundary |
| **S5** | BDD narrow bandwidth + distance control: Same as S4 but restricted to houses within 0.10 miles of boundary | Most restrictive — strongest identification at cost of power |

All specifications use robust (HC1) standard errors clustered at the school attendance zone boundary level.

---

## STEP 3 — FALSIFICATION GATE

I will **REJECT** my hypothesis if ANY of the following occur:

1. **Sign reversal:** The coefficient on test scores in the BDD specifications (S2–S5) is negative.
2. **Statistical insignificance in core BDD:** The coefficient on test scores in S2 (main BDD) has p > 0.10.
3. **BDD estimate exceeds naïve estimate:** If the BDD estimate (S2) is *larger* than the naïve hedonic estimate (S1), this contradicts the theoretical prediction that omitted neighborhood quality biases the naïve estimate upward, casting doubt on the identification strategy.
4. **Instability across bandwidths:** If the BDD estimates in S3–S5 change sign or differ from S2 by more than a factor of 3, suggesting the result is not robust to the local comparison that drives identification.
5. **Falsification on housing characteristics:** If a balance test shows that structural housing characteristics (sq ft, lot size, rooms, age) are discontinuous at the boundary (joint F-test p < 0.05), the identifying assumption of smooth potential outcomes at the boundary is violated.

---

## STEP 4 — R CODE

```r
###############################################################################
# RID Protocol: Willingness to Pay for School Quality — Boundary Discontinuity
# Simulates data consistent with Black (1999, QJE) and runs pre-committed specs
###############################################################################

# --- Load packages ---
library(lfe)        # for felm() with cluster-robust SE and fixed effects
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(20241215)

# =========================================================================
# DATA SIMULATION
# Simulates ~28,000 house sales consistent with the published data description
# =========================================================================

N <- 28000
n_boundaries <- 120  # number of distinct attendance zone boundaries

# Assign each house to a boundary segment
boundary_id <- sample(1:n_boundaries, N, replace = TRUE)

# Distance to boundary (miles): continuous running variable
# Positive = higher-performing school side; Negative = lower-performing school side
distance_to_boundary <- runif(N, -0.50, 0.50)

# Treatment indicator: on the higher-performing school side
higher_school <- as.integer(distance_to_boundary >= 0)

# --- Boundary-level unobserved neighborhood quality ---
# Each boundary has its own baseline price level (neighborhood quality)
boundary_quality <- rnorm(n_boundaries, mean = 0, sd = 0.20)
bq <- boundary_quality[boundary_id]

# --- School test scores ---
# Base school quality differs by boundary; treatment side gets higher scores
# Also correlated with neighborhood quality (source of omitted variable bias)
base_scores <- 50 + 15 * bq + rnorm(n_boundaries, 0, 5)
test_scores_by_boundary <- base_scores[boundary_id]

# Treatment side gets a school quality bump
score_bump <- runif(n_boundaries, 2, 15)  # varies by boundary
test_scores <- test_scores_by_boundary + higher_school * score_bump[boundary_id]

# Normalize test scores to standard deviation units for interpretation
test_scores_sd <- (test_scores - mean(test_scores)) / sd(test_scores)

# --- Housing structural characteristics ---
sqft       <- rnorm(N, 1800, 400) + 50 * bq  # slight correlation w/ neighborhood
lot_size   <- rnorm(N, 0.30, 0.12) + 0.02 * bq
rooms      <- rpois(N, lambda = 6)
age        <- pmax(rnorm(N, 45, 20), 1)
garage     <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.6)
condition  <- sample(1:5, N, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.40, 0.30, 0.10))

# --- Census tract controls ---
median_income <- rnorm(N, 50000, 12000) + 8000 * bq
pct_college   <- pnorm(rnorm(N, 0, 1) + 0.5 * bq)
pct_white     <- pnorm(rnorm(N, 0.5, 0.8) + 0.3 * bq)
crime_rate    <- pmax(rnorm(N, 30, 10) - 5 * bq, 1)

# --- Generate log house prices ---
# True DGP: school quality has a CAUSAL effect of ~3% per SD
# Neighborhood quality has separate large effect (source of OVB in naive regression)
# True causal effect of test scores: 0.03 per SD unit

log_price <- 11.5 +
  0.03 * test_scores_sd +                    # TRUE causal effect of school quality
  0.35 * bq +                                 # neighborhood quality (omitted in naive)
  0.0002 * sqft +
  0.30 * lot_size +
  0.02 * rooms +
  -0.002 * age +
  0.05 * garage +
  0.03 * condition +
  0.000002 * median_income +
  0.10 * pct_college +
  0.05 * pct_white +
  -0.003 * crime_rate +
  0.02 * distance_to_boundary +               # smooth distance effect
  rnorm(N, 0, 0.15)                           # idiosyncratic error

price <- exp(log_price)

# --- Assemble data frame ---
df <- data.frame(
  log_price = log_price,
  price = price,
  test_scores_sd = test_scores_sd,
  test_scores_raw = test_scores,
  distance = distance_to_boundary,
  abs_distance = abs(distance_to_boundary),
  higher_school = higher_school,
  boundary_id = as.factor(boundary_id),
  sqft = sqft,
  lot_size = lot_size,
  rooms = rooms,
  age = age,
  garage = garage,
  condition = condition,
  median_income = median_income,
  pct_college = pct_college,
  pct_white = pct_white,
  crime_rate = crime_rate,
  bq = bq
)

cat("===== DATA SUMMARY =====\n")
cat("N observations:", nrow(df), "\n")
cat("N boundaries:", n_boundaries, "\n")
cat("Mean log price:", round(mean(df$log_price), 3), "\n")
cat("Mean price ($):", round(mean(df$price), 0), "\n")
cat("SD test scores (raw):", round(sd(df$test_scores_raw), 2), "\n\n")

# =========================================================================
# FALSIFICATION / BALANCE TEST
# Test whether housing structural characteristics jump at the boundary
# =========================================================================

cat("===== FALSIFICATION: BALANCE TEST AT BOUNDARY =====\n")
cat("Testing discontinuity in housing characteristics at boundary\n")
cat("(Restricted to houses within 0.20 miles)\n\n")

df_narrow <- df %>% filter(abs_distance <= 0.20)

balance_vars <- c("sqft", "lot_size", "rooms", "age", "garage", "condition")
balance_results <- data.frame(variable = character(), coef = numeric(),
                               se = numeric(), pval = numeric())

for (v in balance_vars) {
  form <- as.formula(paste(v, "~ higher_school | boundary_id | 0 | boundary_id"))
  m <- felm(form, data = df_narrow)
  s <- summary(m)
  balance_results <- rbind(balance_results, data.frame(
    variable = v,
    coef = round(s$coefficients["higher_school", 1], 4),
    se = round(s$coefficients["higher_school", 2], 4),
    pval = round(s$coefficients["higher_school", 4], 4)
  ))
}

print(balance_results)

# Joint F-test via OLS regression of higher_school on all structural vars
joint_test <- lm(higher_school ~ sqft + lot_size + rooms + age + garage + condition,
                 data = df_narrow)
f_stat <- summary(joint_test)$fstatistic
joint_p <- pf(f_stat[1], f_stat[2], f_stat[3], lower.tail = FALSE)
cat("\nJoint F-test: F =", round(f_stat[1], 3), ", p =", round(joint_p, 4), "\n")

if (joint_p < 0.05) {
  cat("*** FALSIFICATION GATE TRIGGERED: Housing characteristics discontinuous at boundary ***\n\n")
} else {
  cat("Balance test PASSED: No evidence of discontinuity in housing characteristics.\n\n")
}

# =========================================================================
# SPECIFICATION S1: Naive Hedonic Regression (no boundary FE)
# =========================================================================

cat("===== SPECIFICATION S1: NAIVE HEDONIC =====\n")

s1 <- felm(log_price ~ test_scores_sd + sqft + lot_size + rooms + age +
             garage + condition + median_income + pct_college +
             pct_white + crime_rate | 0 | 0 | boundary_id,
           data = df)

cat("Coefficient on test_scores_sd (naive):\n")
print(round(summary(s1)$coefficients["test_scores_sd", ], 4))
cat("\n")

# =========================================================================
# SPECIFICATION S2: BDD Baseline — Boundary Fixed Effects, Full Sample
# =========================================================================

cat("===== SPECIFICATION S2: BDD BASELINE (Full Sample, Boundary FE) =====\n")

s2 <- felm(log_price ~ test_scores_sd + sqft + lot_size + rooms + age +
             garage + condition + median_income + pct_college +
             pct_white + crime_rate | boundary_id | 0 | boundary_id,
           data = df)

cat("Coefficient on test_scores_sd (BDD baseline):\n")
print(round(summary(s2)$coefficients["test_scores_sd", ], 4))
cat("\n")

# =========================================================================
# SPECIFICATION S3: BDD — Bandwidth 0.20 miles
# =========================================================================

cat("===== SPECIFICATION S3: BDD (Within 0.20 miles, Boundary FE) =====\n")

df_bw020 <- df %>% filter(abs_distance <= 0.20)

s3 <- felm(log_price ~ test_scores_sd + sqft + lot_size + rooms + age +
             garage + condition + median_income + pct_college +
             pct_white + crime_rate | boundary_id | 0 | boundary_id,
           data = df_bw020)

cat("N observations (0.20 mi):", nrow(df_bw020), "\n")
cat("Coefficient on test_scores_sd (BDD 0.20mi):\n")
print(round(summary(s3)$coefficients["test_scores_sd", ], 4))
cat("\n")

# =========================================================================
# SPECIFICATION S4: BDD — Full Sample with Linear Distance Control
# =========================================================================

cat("===== SPECIFICATION S4: BDD (Full Sample, Boundary FE + Distance Control) =====\n")

s4 <- felm(log_price ~ test_scores_sd + distance + sqft + lot_size + rooms + age +
             garage + condition + median_income + pct_college +
             pct_white + crime_rate | boundary_id | 0 | boundary_id,
           data = df)

cat("Coefficient on test_scores_sd (BDD + distance):\n")
print(round(summary(s4)$coefficients["test_scores_sd", ], 4))
cat("\n")

# =========================================================================
# SPECIFICATION S5: BDD — 0.10 miles + Distance Control
# =========================================================================

cat("===== SPECIFICATION S5: BDD (Within 0.10 miles, Boundary FE + Distance) =====\n")

df_bw010 <- df %>% filter(abs_distance <= 0.10)

s5 <- felm(log_price ~ test_scores_sd + distance + sqft + lot_size + rooms + age +
             garage + condition + median_income + pct_college +
             pct_white + crime_rate | boundary_id | 0 | boundary_id,
           data = df_bw010)

cat("N observations (0.10 mi):", nrow(df_bw010), "\n")
cat("Coefficient on test_scores_sd (BDD 0.10mi + distance):\n")
print(round(summary(s5)$coefficients["test_scores_sd", ], 4))
cat("\n")

# =========================================================================
# SUMMARY TABLE
# =========================================================================

cat("\n===== SUMMARY OF ALL SPECIFICATIONS =====\n\n")

extract_coef <- function(model, label) {
  s <- summary(model)$coefficients
  row <- s["test_scores_sd", ]
  data.frame(
    Specification = label,
    Coefficient = round(row[1], 4),
    Std_Error = round(row[2], 4),
    t_stat = round(row[3], 3),
    p_value = round(row[4], 4)
  )
}

results <- rbind(
  extract_coef(s1, "S1: Naive Hedonic"),
  extract_coef(s2, "S2: BDD Baseline"),
  extract_coef(s3, "S3: BDD 0.20mi"),
  extract_coef(s4, "S4: BDD + Distance"),
  extract_coef(s5, "S5: BDD 0.10mi + Distance")
)

print(results, row.names =

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Boundary discontinuity design (spatial RDD) — running variable is distance from the school attendance zone boundary; houses on either side of the boundary are in the same neighborhood but assigned to different schools; the discontinuity in school quality at the boundary identifies the school quality premium in house prices

key_variables.treatment: assignment to the higher-quality school attendance zone (based on test scores)
key_variables.control: houses on the other side of the boundary, assigned to the lower-quality school

_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Parents value school quality significantly: a one standard deviation increase in test scores (school quality) increases house prices by approximately 2.1% at the attendance boundary, compared to 5-7% in traditional hedonic regressions. The boundary design reveals that roughly 50-70% of the naive school quality premium in hedonic regressions is actually attributable to omitted neighborhood quality rather than school quality. The true willingness to pay for school quality is positive and significant but smaller than previously believed.
_ground_truth.main_effect: A one SD increase in elementary school test scores raises house prices by approximately 2.1% at attendance boundaries (vs. 5-7% in traditional hedonic regressions without boundary FE)
key_robustness: Varying distance bands from boundary (0.05 mile, 0.10 mile, 0.20 mile)
Including boundary fixed effects (comparing only houses on opposite sides of the same boundary)
Controlling for housing characteristics and census tract demographics
Different school quality measures (test scores, expenditures, teacher salaries)
Excluding boundaries that coincide with neighborhood changes (major roads, parks)

identification_strategy_detail.method: Boundary discontinuity design (spatial RDD with boundary fixed effects)
identification_strategy_detail.treatment: School attendance zone assignment (binary: higher-quality vs. lower-quality school side of a boundary)
identification_strategy_detail.estimation_window: Houses within 0.05-0.20 miles of attendance zone boundaries
identification_strategy_detail.unit_of_observation: Individual house sale transaction, geocoded to school attendance zone
identification_strategy_detail.key_assumption: Houses on either side of an attendance zone boundary are in the same neighborhood and differ only in school assignment. The boundary itself does not coincide with other discontinuities (socioeconomic, racial, geographic). Boundary fixed effects absorb any boundary-specific confounds.

key_magnitudes.boundary_premium: +2.1% per SD of test score increase (boundary discontinuity estimate)
key_magnitudes.naive_premium: +5-7% per SD of test score increase (traditional hedonic without boundary FE)
key_magnitudes.bias_share: Approximately 50-70% of the naive premium is attributable to omitted neighborhood quality, not school quality
key_magnitudes.dollar_value: Approximately $4,000-$8,000 premium per house per SD improvement in test scores (in 1990s dollars)

_ground_truth.robustness_notes_detail: Results are robust to distance band choice, boundary fixed effects, and extensive housing and demographic controls. The reduction from 5-7% (naive) to 2.1% (boundary RDD) demonstrates the severity of omitted variable bias in traditional hedonic price regressions. Some boundaries coincide with major roads or natural barriers, which are excluded in robustness checks without materially affecting the estimates.
